\section[o gasóleo]{o gasóleo — diesel (fuel)}

\label{lesson:PT-C404-gasoleo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to honk, then the Portuguese for to mist up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o gasóleo}
\textbf{o gasóleo} — \textquotedblleft{}diesel (fuel)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O meu carro anda a gasóleo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My car runs on diesel.}
\end{quote}

In Brazil: \emph{o diesel}. Petrol is \emph{a gasolina}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gasóleo} is built from \emph{gás} and \emph{óleo} 'oil'; \emph{óleo} goes back to Latin \emph{oleum} 'olive oil' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o gasóleo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o gasóleo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o gasóleo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to honk, then the Portuguese for to mist up, then say \emph{o gasóleo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o gasóleo mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Diesel (fuel)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o combustível]{o combustível — fuel}

\label{lesson:PT-C404-combustivel}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to mist up, then the Portuguese for diesel.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o combustível}
\textbf{o combustível} — \textquotedblleft{}fuel\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O combustível está muito caro este mês.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Fuel is very expensive this month.}
\end{quote}

Also an adjective: \emph{um material combustível}, something that burns.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{combustível} came from French \emph{combustible}, which is built on Latin \emph{combūrere} 'to burn up' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a mangueira]{a mangueira — the hose}

\label{lesson:PT-C404-mangueira}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for diesel, then the Portuguese for fuel.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a mangueira}
\textbf{a mangueira} — \textquotedblleft{}the hose\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O empregado pôs a mangueira no carro.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The attendant put the hose into the car.}
\end{quote}

Also a garden hose. \emph{A mangueira} is the mango tree too, a different word.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mangueira} is built on \emph{manga} 'sleeve' with \emph{-eira}: a long cloth tube. \emph{Manga} is inherited from Latin \emph{manica} 'sleeve' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[abastecer]{abastecer — to fill up (with fuel); to supply}

\label{lesson:PT-C404-abastecer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for fuel, then the Portuguese for the hose.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: abastecer}
\textbf{abastecer} — \textquotedblleft{}to fill up (with fuel); to supply\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Paramos na bomba para abastecer.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We stop at the petrol station to fill up.}
\end{quote}

Also to supply a shop or a town: \emph{abastecer o mercado}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{abastecer} is built from \emph{a-} and Old Portuguese \emph{bastecer} 'to provide', which EtymDB lists. It is usually linked with \emph{bastar} 'to be enough', but the details are not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[atestar]{atestar — to fill to the top; to certify}

\label{lesson:PT-C404-atestar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the hose, then the Portuguese for to fill up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: atestar}
\textbf{atestar} — \textquotedblleft{}to fill to the top; to certify\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Antes de uma viagem longa, ele atesta o depósito.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Before a long trip, he fills the tank to the top.}
\end{quote}

In formal writing, \emph{atestar} also means to certify: \emph{um atestado médico}, a doctor's note.

\begin{cousinweb}
EtymDB gives two sources: the sense 'fill to the top' is built on \emph{testo} 'lid', inherited from Latin \emph{testum}; the sense 'certify' is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{attestārī} 'to bear witness'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
